dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Greg.
Hello, yes. I'm calling about a shed. I manage a property on Malbone Road, 175 Malbone, in the North End, and there's a shed in the back yard.
Okay. What are you looking to do with the shed?

Move it. It's already there, it's not new, I'm not building anything. I just want it moved over to the other side of the yard. So does that need a permit, or not? [pause] I couldn't tell from the website.
Good question. Moving an existing shed can still count, depending on the size and where it ends up. Setbacks from the property line matter. Do you know roughly how big it is?
Size. Um. It's the kind you buy at the store, I think. Ten by eight? Maybe eight by eight. I'd have to go look. As I said before, I'm not the one who put it there.
Sure, that's fine. Smaller ones sometimes get treated differently than bigger ones, so the dimensions will matter. And how far from the fence or the lot line would the new spot be?
I don't know that either. Is that the, what do you call it, the setback? You said that. I don't understand what that is exactly.
Yep. It's the minimum distance a structure has to sit back from the property line. It varies by zone. So the new spot has to meet that, even if the old spot did.
Even if the old spot did. Okay. So if it's moved closer, then there's a problem.

Could be, yes. If it's moved closer to a line than allowed, you'd have an issue. If it stays within the rules, it may be a simpler thing. But I'd want you to apply or at least check before you move it.
Apply for what? The form I found online says shed, and then it has something about accessory structure. Is that the same? Is that the shed permit?
Same family, yeah. A shed is an accessory structure. The permit type you'd be looking at is the shed permit. Just pick shed.
Shed. Okay. [sighs] And does it have to be a licensed contractor who applies? Because I'm not a contractor. I just manage the place for the owner. Does a contractor have to do the paperwork?

Not necessarily. For something like a shed, an owner can usually apply. And if you're acting for the owner, we'd likely want something in writing from them saying you can. If you hire a mover or a contractor, they can apply too, but it isn't a requirement that it be a licensed contractor.
Something in writing. A letter?
A short signed note or an authorization form works. Owner's name, the address, and that you're allowed to handle the permit.
Okay. So the owner writes me a note. And I'm sorry, I'm still not clear. Do I need the permit to move it, or only if it goes somewhere new? It's going somewhere new. But it's the same yard.

Right, so let me say it plainly. Because it's changing location, treat it as needing a permit review. Same yard doesn't automatically make it exempt. Bring the size, a simple sketch of the yard showing the new spot and distances to the lot lines, and the owner's note.

A sketch. I can do a sketch. I just got a raise last month, you know, so I'm still getting used to it, and now I feel like I should be able to afford somebody to draw this. [pause] Sorry, never mind. That's not your problem.
No, it doesn't have to be fancy. Hand-drawn is fine as long as the measurements are on it.
All right. Measurements. And where do I bring this? Is it there at City Hall?
Yes, you can bring it to our office here at City Hall, and we'll take a look. If something's missing, we'll tell you.
And the shed itself, it's not on a foundation. Does that change anything? Or is that something else?
It can matter. Bring that up when you come in, and the inspector can say. If it's just sitting on blocks or the ground, that's usually simpler.
Blocks. I think it's on blocks. I'll check. So just to be sure I have it. Shed permit. Owner's note. Sketch with the measurements. And it doesn't have to be a contractor.
That's it. Plus the size of the shed and where it's going.
Okay. I'm writing it down. Thank you. I'll go look at it this afternoon, I suppose.
Sounds good. Call back if you hit a snag.
I will. Goodbye.
